summary: The new Saleor version enforces uniqueness on User.last_name at the application level (Django model unique=True). During the overlap between deploy_new and retire_old both versions read/write the same rows; the old version can create rows with last_name values that the new version's create operation then rejects with a UNIQUE error because Django's ORM checks for existing rows with the same last_name before inserting. Since pre-existing last_name values cannot be altered and the old version may have already written such values, no zero‑downtime plan can guarantee that both versions remain correct without either changing existing data or preventing the old version from writing duplicates. Therefore the change cannot be safely rolled out in a staged manner.
revision_notes: Root cause: the new app version's model defines last_name as unique. Django's save() performs an existence query for any row with the same last_name; when the old version has already inserted rows with those values, the new version's create raises a UNIQUE violation. The previous plan attempted to add the constraint only after retire_old, but the case.new_create_old_read check failed during deploy_new because the new version immediately encountered the conflict. Without the ability to modify existing last_name values or disable the new version's application‑level uniqueness check, no sequence of SQL and deployment stages can keep both versions correct throughout the overlap.

stages.description: Add a unique constraint on account_user.last_name. This stage is placed after retire_old so that only the new version runs; however it is refused by the runner if earlier checks failed.
sql: ALTER TABLE account_user ADD CONSTRAINT user_last_name_unique UNIQUE (last_name);
